title: Lorenzo's practice before Chicago and the Eighth Illinois audition
summary: Before Chicago, Uncle Papa warned Lorenzo he would meet real musicians, so he drilled alone; at the Eighth Illinois rehearsal he sight-read hard music on one B-flat clarinet and was offered bandmaster, which he declined, and Russell dates the draft to 1918.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years

blocks.x: Do you remember any special exercises that your brother did or anything? When he practiced, did he ever practiced much at home in late days? Or after he learned to play, did he just play on the job and that was about all? Well, I remember when...

One year before you went to Chicago, my uncle Papaya came to him and told him, he said, You're going amongst some great, great musicians. And he said, when you leave here, don't let nobody food. He said, I know you've been a jazz player all your life, so you can play jazz. But you're going to meet some men that really do know music. And he said, you might confront with that. And sure enough, that's what he did. He got on in the room by himself. He didn't ask nobody for nothing. He just came in there and locked himself in the room. And he got all the music that he knew of, such as all the orchestration that my daddy had, and he had a beautiful number of Sally. And for at least an hour, an hour, an hour and a half, he'd run the scale, dramatic scale, tune through, up and down, up and down. He'd get out and went and take a drink of water. Do even sisters, come back there again, sit down and probably look at the paper, get back up and try and do the same thing. But when he went to Illinois, that's why I tell you he had an opportunity of being a bandwriter in the 8 Illinois, in that position as a first lieutenant. He met the bandmaster of the 8 Illinois, and they offered him to play at a rehearsal one Sunday. And he did, he went to, well they were looking for him with a whole caster instrument. You understand? They were looking for him with a whole family of clarinets, A, B flat, B and C. Well he didn't, he went there with his B flat clarinet, his mouthpiece, in his cool pocket here. stuff

That's something to laugh at. That's the truth. And his clarinet, his belt, he had it in his coat pocket, and his two parts of his clarinet wrapped in those steps. Well, you know what kind of impression that must have made on that bandmaster? Yeah, it was funny. What kind of clarinet play out like that? Yeah! You understand? And he told me that there stuck a piece of music, one of the hardest things that he ever read in his life, played in his life. And he came out there and he played that thing with that B-flat clarinet. And when he did, my bandmaster came out there and after this number was over and shook his hand and asked him what conservatory that he attended. He told me I never been to conservatory in my life. Who taught you? My father and my uncle taught you. Man, you're one of the greatest of the years. How do you do it? Out of all these men, out of these clarinet plays I got here, they can't do it. How do you do it? Well, I learnt that that way. Well, I'll give you a position as first, I'll give you band rider and I'll give you first lieutenant in the A's Illinois. Okay, no, I'm going back home. My brother's going to Norman. Well, his wife was about to have a baby. He came back home. Well, instead of me being sent to Norman, I didn't. I had my mother and I had my sister here and I had another one, two more of them, one of them that's dead and one that's living down on Rydell Street. Well, they were young and my father was dead and I wasn't so put.
Well, I was put in class 3B. That would be about 1918, the first world. That's the first world war. How many children did your brother have? Are they still living?
